strengths: Novel conceptual connection between computational reducibility from theoretical CS and transfer learning for CO problems, providing interesting theoretical motivation for task selection
Comprehensive experimental design with systematic progression from pairwise to multi-task transfer, leave-one-out validation, and honest discussion of when/why transfer fails
Technically sound methodology: proper use of Ising-based energy formulations, clear problem specifications, GCON architecture validation, and consistent performance improvements on individual tasks
Multi-task results demonstrate genuine transfer viability: leave-one-out experiments show most tasks fine-tune faster than training from scratch, suggesting shared representations are learnable
High reproducibility standards: promised code release, detailed method descriptions, multiple runs with standard deviations, and transparent reporting of limitations
weaknesses: Core hypothesis incompletely validated: MIS↔MVC transfer works but involves no graph topology change; MIS→MaxClique fails with frozen backbones despite polynomial reduction; K-coloring transfers well despite different linear orbits; MDS shows negative transfer—collectively these undermine claims that reducibility predicts transferability

Weak theory-practice connection: authors acknowledge reducibility-transferability links are 'not trivial' and 'further work is needed'—this significantly weakens the central claim. Task selection in final backbone (Sec. 5.2) relies more on empirical observation than theoretical guidance

Limited experimental scope: evaluation restricted to small synthetic instances (RB-small, BA-small) with no large-scale testing; missing comparisons with related multi-task CO methods (GOAL, UniCO, etc.) mentioned in related work; unfair training regimen (baselines 200-700 epochs vs. fine-tuned models 20-200 epochs)

Inconsistent empirical results that appear cherry-picked: MaxClique shows minimal improvement (4.31→4.32); MDS shows negative transfer; Table 6 suggests task selection was guided by empirical results rather than reducibility theory; leave-one-out experiments use only 20 epochs of fine-tuning, which is extremely limited

Incomplete analysis of transferability mechanisms: no visualization of learned representations or embedding space analysis; limited explanation for why K-coloring transfers better than theoretically closer problems; no mechanistic understanding beyond 'distribution shift'; no evidence that reducibility guides task selection better than random selection

Incremental technical contributions: GCON from Wenkel et al. (2025), energy losses from Lucas (2014), decoder from Karalias & Loukas (2020); main contribution is applying these with transfer strategies—somewhat straightforward application of existing components

Missing critical comparisons and ablations: no statistical significance testing despite reporting standard deviations; no comparison of reducibility-based vs. other task selection heuristics; unclear hyperparameter tuning procedure (A/B parameters); duality gap explanation in Sec. 4.1 suggests theoretical assumptions don't hold well in practice but is not adequately addressed

strengths: Novel idea connecting computational reducibility to transfer learning across domains
Comprehensive empirical study of pairwise and multi-task transfer scenarios with ablations
Honest discussion of limitations and failure modes (e.g., 'theoretical equivariance alone is not enough')
Solid experimental methodology with multiple runs, error bars, and baseline comparisons
Well-motivated problem: understanding transferability for neural combinatorial optimization
weaknesses: Central thesis weakly supported: computational reducibility fails to predict transferability in key cases (MIS↔MaxClique, MDS), contradicting the main claim
Mixed empirical results: pairwise transfer often underperforms baselines; multi-task improvements are marginal and inconsistent across tasks (MDS shows zero benefit)

Confounded experimental design: varying training budgets (20/200/700 epochs) across sections makes it unclear whether improvements come from transfer or longer training; only small graphs (RB-small, BA-small) evaluated
Post-hoc task selection: pretraining set chosen based on empirical results (Table 6) rather than theoretical reducibility, weakening the core argument
Limited scope: only 6 synthetic tasks, no real-world graphs, unclear scaling to larger problems; results don't justify claims about 'foundational models'
Insufficient analysis of failure modes: paper identifies that distribution shift matters more than reducibility structure but doesn't reconcile this with the central hypothesis
Unfair comparisons in multi-task section: fine-tuned models (20 epochs) compared to baselines (200 epochs) don't demonstrate practical advantages
Gap between theory and practice: paper provides no mechanistic explanation for why or when computational complexity relationships should predict neural network transferability

strengths: Novel conceptual bridge between computational reducibility and transfer learning, connecting theory to practice in an underexplored way
Comprehensive experimental progression across individual tasks, pairwise transfer, and multi-task learning with systematic research questions
Honest treatment of theory-practice gaps: authors transparently explain when reducibility-guided transfer succeeds or fails (e.g., duality gap, distribution shift)
Strong technical execution including improved MaxClique results, careful ablation studies, and practical optimizations (parallelized decoder)
Valuable leave-one-out multi-task results showing 5/6 tasks benefit from pretraining; fine-tuning on 3-task backbone matches 200-epoch single-task training in 20 epochs
Good reproducibility: detailed methods, clear presentation of error bars, promised open-source code
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: GCON, energy-based losses, and decoders are from prior work; contribution is primarily application rather than new methods

Loose theory-practice connection: promised reducibility-transfer link is inconsistent; title overstates findings ('can lead to' vs. proven causal relationship); Table 4 shows MIS→MaxClique transfer substantially underperforms baseline

Critical gap: no comparison with related multi-task CO solvers (GOAL, UniCO, recent RL-based methods), making it unclear whether benefits derive from reducibility-guided task selection or simply multi-task learning
Limited experimental scope: only small graphs (206-node RB, ~100-node BA), 6 tasks, unsupervised setting only; scalability to real-world problems unclear

Incomplete analysis of key phenomena: unexplained underperformance of MaxClique and MDS in multi-task setting; MDS sometimes performs worse with fine-tuning; backbone selection appears ad-hoc despite theory motivation; no ablation on pretraining set choices

Experimental design issues: different training lengths across conditions (700 vs. 200 epochs), high variance in some results (K-coloring: 61.92±36.11), only 5 runs per condition, no statistical significance testing

No systematic characterization of when reducibility predicts transfer success; Filar et al.'s linear orbit concept mentioned but never operationalized; missing generalization analysis on held-out graph types/sizes
Foundation model claims insufficiently supported: only 6-task backbone shown; unclear if approach scales; practical benefits are modest (comparable, not superior, performance)

strengths: Novel conceptual contribution bridging computational reducibility from theoretical CS with neural transferability in deep learning
Thorough experimental investigation progressing systematically from single-task baselines to pairwise transfer to multi-task learning with detailed analysis
Honest and candid treatment of limitations, acknowledging that theoretical reductions don't directly translate to parameter transfer and that some connections remain non-trivial
Solid experimental methodology with multiple runs, error bars, appropriate controls, and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Practical insights on effective pretraining task selection (MDS, MIS, K-coloring) and systematic comparison showing multi-task learning outperforms unified-task reduction approaches
Technical soundness of GNN encoder, energy-based losses, and sequential decoder with parallelized k-seeding construction
weaknesses: Central thesis undermined by empirical results: the paper's core claim that reducibility should inform transferability is demonstrated to be indirect and non-trivial, with frozen representations failing across non-topology-preserving reductions (Table 4) and MDS showing zero transfer benefit (Table 5)

Weak evidence that reducibility-based task selection outperforms simpler alternatives: task selection for pretraining (Sec 5.2) is post-hoc rationalization rather than theory-driven prediction, with no comparison to random or diversity-based selection strategies

Limited experimental scope confined to synthetic graphs (RB, BA) with 200-1200 nodes; zero-shot DIMACS results show large gaps from best-known solutions (e.g., MANN_a81: 300 vs. 1100); no evaluation on real-world problem instances

Incremental practical improvements with 20-epoch fine-tuning not matching 200-epoch full training (Table 7), often within noise margins; missing empirical comparisons to recent multi-task CO baselines (GOAL, UniCO, Li et al. 2025, Wang et al. 2025)

Architectural confound: GCON significantly outperforms other GNNs (Table 2) but contribution of architecture vs. transfer strategy not isolated; loss function choice (Hamiltonian vs. Motzkin-Strauss) shown crucial but not systematically studied across transfer scenarios

Experimental design issues: (1) baselines trained for 700 epochs vs. 200 for fine-tuned models (Table 4) confounds comparison; (2) task selection justified post-hoc using experimental results (Table 6) leading to potential circularity; (3) early stopping criteria and train/val/test splits incompletely specified

Poor support from linear orbit framework: K-coloring—placed in different linear orbit by Filar et al.—transfers poorly (Tables 5, 7), directly contradicting the reducibility hypothesis without satisfactory explanation

Missing critical ablations: no comparison to random pretraining task selection, no study of necessary number of pretraining tasks, decoder k-parameter impact not isolated, impact of A/B hyperparameter tuning across transfer scenarios absent

strengths: Novel conceptual contribution connecting computational reducibility from complexity theory to neural transfer learning, well-motivated in introduction
Comprehensive experimental design spanning pairwise transferability, leave-one-out multi-task learning, and multiple datasets with ablation studies
Honest and transparent discussion of failure modes and theory-practice gaps (e.g., Section 4.2, Appendix C)
Thorough implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, and reproducibility considerations
Well-structured presentation with clear section organization and appropriate use of visualizations
weaknesses: Core hypothesis inadequately supported: Appendix C demonstrates that explicitly applying computational reductions produces worse results than multi-task learning on original graphs, directly contradicting the main claim
Leave-one-out results (Table 5) suggest task similarity benefits transfer roughly equally regardless of formal reduction relationships, undermining reducibility-specific claims
Missing theoretical justification for why polynomial-time reductions from complexity theory should improve gradient-based neural transfer learning on finite data
Inconsistent empirical findings: Table 6 shows MDS performs best when reducibly-similar tasks are excluded; K-coloring (not linearly reducible per Filar et al. 2019) works well in pretraining
Limited technical novelty: GCON architecture, energy-based losses, and sequential decoder all from prior work; main contribution is empirical investigation

Narrow experimental scope: all on synthetic graphs (200-1200 nodes); no comparison to recent multi-task CO methods (GOAL, UniCO, Sanokowski et al. 2024); zero-shot DIMACS results show large optimality gaps
Task selection in Section 5.2 appears ad-hoc (empirical observation of what works) rather than principled application of reducibility insights
Paper framed as validating reducibility-guided transfer but actually demonstrates that straightforward multi-task learning on original graphs outperforms reduction-based approaches

strengths: Novel conceptual connection between computational reducibility (TCS) and neural transfer learning, well-motivated and relatively unexplored
Comprehensive experimental design with systematic progression from pairwise to multi-task transferability, including leave-one-out studies and extensive appendices
Honest, nuanced discussion of when and why transfer fails (e.g., topology-changing reductions causing distribution shift), strengthening credibility
Detailed technical analysis of failure modes, particularly Section 4.2's explanation of why frozen-backbone MIS→MaxClique transfer breaks due to complement graph properties
Practical multi-task results demonstrating that fine-tuning on 3-task backbone for 20 epochs achieves competitive performance with 200-epoch single-task training
Reproducibility strengths: promised open-source code, detailed hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and decoder specifications throughout appendices
Thorough Appendix C comparison of multi-task vs. unified-task reduction approaches, providing valuable empirical insights on practical limitations of graph reductions
weaknesses: Central theoretical connection is loose: reducibility motivates the work but is never formalized; no principled framework for predicting which tasks will transfer based on reduction structure, and authors acknowledge 'connections are not trivial'

Modest practical improvements: GCON gains over baselines are incremental (Table 2); fine-tuned models sometimes underperform full training (Table 7); MDS shows no benefit from transfer; improvements often within noise margins
Critical omission of experimental comparison with existing multi-task CO methods (GOAL, UniCO, UniCO2, Li et al. 2025, Wang et al. 2025), limiting evidence that this approach outperforms baselines
Limited dataset diversity: only synthetic RB and BA graphs (200-1200 nodes); real-world applicability unclear; DIMACS evaluation only in appendix with zero-shot evaluation

Experimental design concerns: baselines trained for 200-700 epochs vs. fine-tuned models for 20-200 epochs in different regimes, making transfer benefits difficult to isolate from training duration effects

MIS→MaxClique results contradict reducibility hypothesis: frozen backbone fails catastrophically even with 'true reduction' (Experiment #10); Graph Transformer additions (#8-9) show only marginal improvements; suggests learned representations don't capture reduction structure
Leave-one-out results (Table 5) show highly inconsistent transfer benefits across tasks (MDS shows degradation), inconsistent with a unified framework
No formal analysis of what properties of reductions enable neural transfer, or principled method to predict transfer success; post-hoc task selection (Table 6) not grounded in reduction structure
